item.title: Daily scan · 17 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 17 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

16 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

OpenAI signs four assessors for internal alignment and safety reviews

OpenAI signed agreements with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire to assess alignment and safeguards using internal systems and evidence. The work includes examining a frontier reinforcement-learning run and checking the quality and coverage of post-training evaluations. This gives evaluators access beyond public model tests, but the announcement reports plans rather than completed findings, and publication remains subject to confidentiality redactions and possible disclosure delays.

Source: OpenAI / Goodfire / Transluce · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date; corroborated by Goodfire and Transluce announcements.

Limits: Planned assessments, not completed safety findings; negotiated access and publication restrictions; Apollo and Goodfire receive non-outcome-contingent compensation

Read scope: Official OpenAI announcement, protocol and compensation footnotes; downloaded Goodfire announcement and full Transluce pilot terms; no assessment findings or underlying models inspected

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#openai-embedded-assessments

OpenAI announcement and terms: https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/

Goodfire announcement: https://www.goodfire.com/blog/announcing-our-collaboration-with-openai

Transluce pilot access and publication limits: https://transluce.org/embedded-assessment-pilot-with-openai

Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training

This study asks whether a fixed annotation budget is better spent on human or AI-generated preferences. It trains three small language-model families on helpfulness and summarization, matching estimated data costs instead of example counts. Synthetic data performs better at shared budgets and peaks early; human data catches up only in some higher-budget tests. The comparison uses estimated labor and serving prices and AI judges, so its dollar thresholds are specific to this setup.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-12 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Estimated annotation labor and proxy serving prices; 7–8B models with LoRA; AI-judged helpfulness and summarization

Read scope: Submission history; data, cost and evaluation methods; main results; limitations and selected appendices; official code README inspected; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#human-or-synthetic

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16895

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.16895v1

Official code: https://github.com/shourikb/human-or-synthetic

Synthetic preference data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/liteshadow4/synthetic-pref-tulu3

Benchleaking: Benchmark recall in base models

Qin and colleagues tested whether base language models could reproduce benchmark questions and answers absent from their prompts. They found large differences across four models and recalculated scores with recalled examples marked wrong. This gives evaluation teams a way to check whether high scores depend on recall, although some closely related question pairs can be reconstructed without previous exposure.

Source: Yiwei Qin and coauthors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 16:10:16 UTC.

Limits: Observed matches need benchmark-specific interpretation: WinoGrande twin questions can be reconstructed without exposure. The adjusted score is a conservative scoring rule, not a causal estimate of a model's ability without contamination. Author-linked code returned 404 when checked.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, continuation-audit method, score construction and matching-rules appendix in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#benchleaking

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21315

Full paper, including matching rules: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21315v1

Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

A model can earn a higher training reward while giving worse reasons for a decision. This study creates access-control tasks whose correct reasons can be computed exactly, then trains models with deliberately imperfect checkers while measuring the true score. Some checkers reward padding explanations with irrelevant details; others stop providing useful feedback or mainly add noise. The patterns recur across the authors' training configurations, but the size of the damage does not, and the tasks use bounded policy abstractions.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Bounded authorization-policy testbed and abstracted public policies; damage magnitude did not replicate across the authors' configurations; artifact release not verified

Read scope: Submission history; oracle and verifier construction; main results, replication findings, limitations and selected appendices; code availability statement inspected; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#optimistic-verifiers

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21538

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21538v1

Toloka Arena adds ten-category failure profiles for enterprise agents

Toloka added failure profiles to its Arena, showing ten kinds of mistakes rather than only an overall score. It reports that about half of failed attempts among the ten leading models passed a conversation assessment even though system records were wrong. The profiles can help teams choose what to test or retrain, but these are results from Toloka's simulated workflows.

Source: Toloka · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date (article and dated HTML metadata).

Limits: Company-run simulated enterprise workflows; error categories can overlap; reported rates are shares of all attempts rather than mutually exclusive shares of failures

Read scope: Full official product/research post and stated scoring definitions; raw trajectories and grading code not inspected; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#toloka-arena-failure-profiles

Toloka failure-profile release and scoring definitions: https://toloka.ai/blog/what-the-scores-dont-tell-you-about-ai-agents-on-toloka-arena/

Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning

When a cheap safety checker sends only uncertain answers to a stronger judge, confidently missed harm escapes review. This paper tests how that weakness changes during training and after the checker is updated. Confidently missed harmful answers often become a larger share of remaining harm even when their total amount falls. The proposed checks distinguish these trends, but evidence covers two small models and two reward judges, and human review sometimes disagrees with automated measures.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Two 7–8B policies, one commercial judge and one open guard, mainly two seeds; limited human audit; helpfulness trade-offs vary by model

Read scope: Submission history; validation protocol; reward conditions, experimental setup, results, limitations and human-audit appendix; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#jev-as-a-reward

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20955

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20955v1

Prolific adds a visual editor for multimodal data collection and evaluation

Prolific has renamed AI Task Builder to Task Builder and added a drag-and-drop editor with the same capabilities as its API. Teams can collect or compare text, images, audio and video, including feedback tied to individual video frames. This consolidates evaluation setup, but the announcement does not provide a controlled comparison of data quality or turnaround time.

Source: Prolific · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date; corroborated by the product-update index.

Limits: An expansion of an existing product, not a newly created participant network; no controlled quality or speed comparison

Read scope: Full dated official release, feature descriptions and availability statement; product not executed and participant quality not independently tested

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#prolific-task-builder

Prolific Task Builder release: https://www.prolific.com/resources/evaluate-and-collect-text-images-audio-and-video-with-task-builder

Official product-update index: https://www.prolific.com/resources?type=product-updates

GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model

This model judges a reasoning step using earlier steps and their assessments plus the rest of the proposed solution. It learns to check consistency, the step itself and whether the solution stays on task. The authors report better error detection and guided mathematics search, but checking unfinished candidates requires generating their remaining steps, increasing cost. Tests of whether this improves complete interactive agent tasks remain future work.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Online search must complete candidate trajectories; cost ablation reports +71.7% tokens and +42.4% latency; interactive agent success not tested

Read scope: Submission history; model and dataset construction; main benchmark results, test-time search, inference-cost analysis and selected appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#gprm

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20755

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20755v1

Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization

Liu and colleagues built 32 tasks that ask coding agents to speed up working scientific programs while keeping their outputs correct. Agents can test changes during development, but a separate checker measures the final program. The reported results show that build settings and interacting code changes can matter greatly; the scores describe complete agent setups on fixed CPU workloads, so they do not isolate model ability.

Source: Bowen Liu and coauthors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 10:52:59 UTC.

Limits: Scores mix model, harness and compute choices; the main table uses one run per agent, with repeats for two. Speedups are relative to differently tuned task baselines at fixed CPU workloads; trajectory analyses use older v1.0 runs.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, benchmark construction, scoring protocol, main results and limitations in HTML; official project page; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#accelerate-bench

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20882

Full paper, benchmark protocol and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20882v1

Official project, reported results and access requirements: https://acceleratebench.com/

Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data

Kua and Song tested whether generated images help when the image generator learns only from the same training set as the classifier. Across six datasets, benefits were generally smaller when generated images differed more from real ones or the starting classifier was already strong. Ordinary image transformations matched most of the largest gains under equal training steps, so generating more images was not automatically worthwhile.

Source: Daniel Kua and Yan Song · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 17:47:45 UTC.

Limits: The estimated mismatch is a lower bound, and the theoretical bound explains trends without predicting gain magnitude or direction; stability and dependence terms remain unquantified. Results do not test externally pretrained generators.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, experimental setup, theoretical-bound interpretation, equal-step augmentation comparison and conclusion in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#generative-augmentation-no-external-data

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21467

Full paper and experiment protocol: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21467v1

Policy Optimization With Multiple Verifiers via Pareto Rankings

When several checks score an answer, counting passed checks can hide which requirements improved. POLPO trains on comparisons where one answer passes every check another answer passes, plus at least one more; it leaves conflicting cases unordered. The authors report gains in coding and following multiple instructions. The method receives no learning signal when none of the sampled answers clearly improves on another, and some coding tests use only one training seed.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-14 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: No dominance means no comparison signal; APPS and AceCode use one training seed; benefits depend on automatic checks and small-model benchmark settings

Read scope: Submission history; partial-order objective; coding and instruction-following result tables; conclusion, reproducibility statement and selected computation/evaluation appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#polpo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19064

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19064v1

SAJ-MTL: Modeling demographic differences in annotation

Gupta and colleagues built a model that keeps track of which demographic groups label a post and which groups the post targets. This preserves differences in how people judge harmful text and lets users choose how to weight those views. The authors report better predictions on two datasets, but groups with sparse data were excluded and the method does not guarantee fair moderation.

Source: Soumyajit Gupta, Maria De-Arteaga and Matthew Lease · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 17:42:54 UTC.

Limits: Experiments cover two toxicity datasets and four race groups; three Measuring Hate Speech groups were omitted because annotator-target pairs were sparse. Group attributes remain sensitive, and improved prediction does not guarantee fairness.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, methods overview, dataset and label protocol, results tables, discussion and ethical considerations in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#saj-mtl

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21458

Full paper and results tables: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21458v1

micro1 describes fixing infrastructure errors that distorted agent evaluations

micro1 describes changes to the system that runs and grades its AI-agent evaluations. It now separates infrastructure failures from wrong answers, retries failed attempts and checks each model's actual output limits before a benchmark run. The company reports that correcting one token-limit problem raised a model's score from 0.33 to 0.48, but this is an internal case study rather than independently reproduced evidence.

Source: micro1 · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date; retrospective about earlier infrastructure changes.

Limits: Engineering retrospective, not a new product launch; anonymous model and benchmark in cited score example; internal measurements not independently reproduced

Read scope: Full official engineering report, especially failure handling, frozen task versions and release-day harness limits; infrastructure and score corrections not executed or independently audited

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#micro1-rollout-reliability

micro1 engineering report: https://www.micro1.ai/blog/the-only-bottleneck-should-be-the-model

Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment

Preference training usually stores intermediate model activity for backpropagation, which consumes GPU memory. This method uses differences between preferred and rejected answers to choose a small set of directions for trying weight changes without backpropagation. The authors report similar judged answer preferences to standard training while using about 59% less peak memory at 2,048 tokens. It needs three forward passes per update, so lower memory does not establish faster training; evidence covers one small model and dataset.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: One Qwen2.5-1.5B model and HH-RLHF dataset; LLM judges; three forward passes per update; no demonstrated speed advantage

Read scope: Submission history; optimization method; experimental setup; complete pairwise and memory results; limitations and hyperparameter/evaluation appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#ca-zodpo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20635

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20635v1

Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows

Bathla built six simulated environments for Indian travel, payments, tax, forms and customer support. Their 321 public tasks are checked by written rules that recompute results from made-up records. This lets teams inspect why an agent passed without relying on another AI judge. The reported tests use one run per task, and the simplified rules and partly machine-produced language examples limit what the scores show about real services.

Source: Daksh Bathla / Navital Labs · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 11:35:01 UTC; new paper about software first released 27 Oct 2026.

Limits: Trip scores include one format-repair retry; some results use earlier grader versions. The rules simplify practice, and the Tamil, Bengali and Marathi examples were not reviewed by native speakers. Private held-out tasks are not inspectable.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, environment definitions, grader protocol, reported results and limitations in HTML; official repository README and GitHub release metadata; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#navital-gym

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20924

Full paper, grader details and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20924v1

Official code, tasks and license: https://github.com/Navitallabs/navital-gym

Initial software release, dated 27 Oct 2026: https://github.com/Navitallabs/navital-gym/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Surge compares coding agents on engineering judgment

Surge tested five coding agents on its sudo L7 benchmark, which evaluates engineering judgment as well as working code. It reports that all three Claude models outscored the two GPT models, with similar functional correctness but larger differences in communication and spotting hidden risks. These company-run results have not been independently reproduced and do not establish how the agents will perform on other workloads.

Source: Surge AI · 2026-11-13 · Original publication date (article and publication metadata).

Limits: Company-run comparison; exact task count and agent software assignment are not reported in the reviewed article body; results not independently reproduced

Read scope: Official article body, examples and current web extraction; chart scores not transcribed; exact task count and model-to-harness assignment not verified; tasks, rubrics and runs not independently audited or reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#surge-sudo-l7-model-comparison

Surge comparison and evaluation setup: https://surgehq.ai/blog/claude-vs-gpt-software-engineering

item.title: Daily scan · 16 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 16 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

18 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting

A preferred answer can contain mistakes, and a rejected answer can still contain useful text. PORT compares how likely the model considers small pieces of each answer and uses their ranks within a training batch to change how strongly those pieces affect learning. The aim is to learn from imperfect preference labels without letting unreliable pieces dominate; the method was less reliable with very small batches.

Source: PORT authors · 2026-11-09 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Small-batch sensitivity; sufficient theory assumptions; multi-turn extension untested

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#port

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12763

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.12763v1

Code: https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT

VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization

Image-answering models can mention objects that are absent, especially when answering in languages with less training data. VEPO uses English questions to locate key image regions, then trains with the same answer paired with either the full image or an image with those regions hidden. This encourages answers backed by visible evidence in other languages. The reported tests cover Chinese, French and Hindi; Hindi training also needed English examples.

Source: VEPO authors · 2026-11-13 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: English-centric transfer; Hindi required English-pair mixing

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#vepo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18096

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18096v1

PrivacyPR: Real-world privacy fixes for code-review evaluation

PrivacyPR tests whether AI code reviewers can spot problems that expose or misuse personal information. It turns real privacy fixes accepted by developers into review tasks by putting the faulty code back. Asking agents to focus on privacy helped them find more problems, but they still raised false alarms and some dataset labels were uncertain.

Source: PrivacyPR authors · 2026-11-13 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Small evaluation subset; both annotators endorsed 72% of automated GDPR-principle labels

Read scope: Abstract and submission history; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#privacypr

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18293

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18293v1

Mercor announces $750 million Series D at a $20 billion valuation

Mercor announced a $750 million funding deal at a $20 billion valuation. It says the financing will support tools that use human expertise to train AI agents and test them on realistic workplace tasks. The deal includes employee share sales, and Mercor did not say how much is new money for the business.

Source: Mercor · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date.

Limits: Primary-versus-secondary capital split undisclosed; funding and valuation are not revenue

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#mercor-series-d

Mercor announcement: https://www.mercor.com/blog/series-d/

Reuters reporting: https://www.aol.com/articles/ai-training-startup-mercor-valued-153730000.html

FlinkEval: Synthetic data for streaming-SQL evaluation

FlinkEval tests whether AI can write database queries for data that keeps arriving, such as a stream of transactions. It creates requests and matching queries, then checks them on a working streaming database. This reveals problems with timing and unclear requests, but some reported scores judge query quality even when the queries could not run.

Source: FlinkEval authors · 2026-11-12 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Single deployment; five-model study excluded 115 windowing cases affected by an engine defect; 81 background DML cases not executable, scored by judged SQL quality

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#flinkeval

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17093

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.17093v1

Scale and Singapore's IMDA introduce SG-LegalClarify

SG-LegalClarify tests whether AI asks for missing facts before answering questions about Singapore law. Models can ask a simulated user for details, and AI judges check their answers against criteria written by legal experts. The results reveal gaps in gathering facts and applying the law, but the score counts individual criteria rather than fully correct answers.

Source: Scale / IMDA · 2026-11-12 · Original publication date.

Limits: Reported criterion-satisfaction scores are not overall legal accuracy; jurisdiction-specific and partly AI-judged

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#sg-legalclarify

Scale research report: https://scale.com/blog/scale-imda-legal-reasoning-benchmark

Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling

This paper asks whether clues about how people read can help a model judge which answer people would prefer. It predicts how long a reader might look at each word, spreads that signal to nearby words, and adds it to an answer-scoring model. The reported gains concern preference prediction in English; the study uses predicted gaze, not new eye-tracking measurements, and does not test whether it improves a chatbot's answers.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-10 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: English-only experiments; synthetic gaze; no downstream policy-alignment test

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#gaze-reward-modeling

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13477

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.13477v1

Nemotron-PII-Japan: Annotated synthetic Japanese business documents

NVIDIA created made-up Japanese business documents to help train and test systems that find or hide personal information. The process chooses fictional identifying details, builds documents around them and labels where those details appear. This provides examples without collecting customer documents, but the labels do not cover every relevant detail and can contain mistakes.

Source: NVIDIA · 2026-11-09 · Announcement 9 Nov; dataset card release date 10 Nov 2026.

Limits: Annotations are not exhaustive; no fixed public train/test split

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#nemotron-pii-japan

Official release article: https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-pii-japan

Dataset & license: https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII-Japan

Labelbox and Wipro partner on RL environments and managed enterprise agents

Labelbox and Wipro announced a partnership to help businesses train, test and use AI agents on workplace tasks. They say Wipro will help customers connect their systems and define what good work looks like, while Labelbox supplies simulated practice environments and agents that carry out tasks. The companies have not published customer results showing measurable gains from the partnership.

Source: Labelbox / Wipro · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date.

Limits: No named customer outcomes, deployment counts or measured production gains disclosed

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#labelbox-wipro

Original press release: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/labelbox-partners-with-wipro-to-scale-adoption-of-ai-agents-that-learn-from-enterprise-experience-302934232.html

Labelbox details: https://labelbox.com/blog/labelbox-wipro-partnership/

MotionGraphicsBench: Programmatic checks for generated animations

MotionGraphicsBench tests whether AI can animate supplied artwork according to a designer's instructions. Instead of comparing the result with one reference animation, readable checking programs test requested movements, timing and other properties. This allows different valid solutions and makes failures easier to inspect, but the checks measure following instructions rather than how beautiful an animation looks.

Source: Figma research · 2026-11-07 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC); release article 10 Nov 2026.

Limits: Narrow SVG motion-editing task; pass/fail measures instruction compliance rather than aesthetic quality

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#motiongraphicsbench

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10592

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10592v1

Official release article: https://huggingface.co/blog/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench

AERO: Adaptive Ensemble-Disagreement Routing for Oracle Feedback in Sample-Efficient Online RLHF

Asking for a preference judgment on every training example can be expensive. AERO lets several answer-scoring models vote: when they disagree strongly, it requests an outside judgment; when they agree, it supplies a predicted preference itself. This focuses the feedback budget on examples where the models are uncertain. The experiments used a fixed AI scoring model as the outside judge, so the reported savings still need testing with human feedback.

Source: AERO authors · 2026-11-07 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Deterministic reward-model oracle; no real human-feedback evaluation

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#aero

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10750

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10750v1

Code: https://github.com/Shrey-Singhal/AERO

Shaping Useful Noise: An energy-distribution audit for synthetic images

This paper asks how to choose useful synthetic images for training visual models. It compares the distributions of confidence scores that the same image model assigns to real and synthetic images. The comparison helped predict training results, but its proposed image selection method was checked using an existing model's features and still needs testing through new model training.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-09 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Curation intervention reports frozen-feature proxies; matched pretraining remains future work

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#shaping-useful-noise

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11962

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.11962v1

Turing describes turning connected company archives into RL benchmarks

Turing describes turning connected company records into simulated workplaces where AI agents can practice real tasks. It says automated checks score the work, letting AI labs train and test agents using the context found across a company's files, messages and code. The post explains the program without giving a launch date, test results or an independent privacy audit.

Source: Turing · 2026-11-11 · Program explanation published 11 Nov; launch date unspecified.

Limits: Program explanation; no new customer, dataset size, benchmark score or privacy audit disclosed

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#turing-company-archives

Turing program details: https://www.turing.com/blog/company-data-ai-benchmarks

OmniSynth: Stress-testing synthetic-health-data quality metrics

OmniSynth checks how well synthetic health records preserve real data patterns, including which values are missing. It deliberately adds flaws to data to see whether measures of similarity, privacy and usefulness notice the changes. This helps expose misleading quality scores, but some measures were unstable, fairness checks are absent and testing of usefulness for later prediction tasks remains incomplete.

Source: OmniSynth authors · 2026-11-09 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Some classifier metrics were unstable; utility stress tests and fairness metrics remain incomplete

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#omnisynth

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11888

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.11888v1

Surge reports targeted RL gains for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

Surge tested whether focused reinforcement learning could improve Nemotron on tasks such as coding, following detailed instructions and using tools. Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

Reasoning models sometimes keep working after they have enough information to finish. LoCo finds these points and trains the model to prefer a shorter, checked continuation over its original longer continuation, with both starting from the same reasoning so far. This teaches where to conclude, potentially cutting the cost of generating answers. The reported tests preserve or improve accuracy on mathematics and code; benefits on tasks without checkable answers remain unproven.

See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models

Masked diffusion language models build text by repeatedly filling in missing pieces. Their training estimates a learning signal from text blocks, but random selection can repeat some blocks and miss others. This paper evaluates every block once and averages the results, reducing that source of noise and improving the reported tests on one model. Its proposed use with PPO or DPO, methods used to learn from preference feedback, remains untested.
